Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results.", "page": 16}, {"text": "Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective.", "page": 15}]}]

{"text": "In the realm of adolescent social network research, the correlation between substance use and friendship formation is well-documented. Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results [47]. Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective. This finding not only underscores a fundamental lack of theoretical understanding regarding developmental relationship patterns within this demographic but also signals the urgent need to explore more deeply the factors influencing relational dynamics among AI youth. Because the conventional assumption in much of the adolescent health literature, that risky behavior is a primary determinant of relationships in youth, does not hold in our study, which may also mean that common network intervention strategies aimed at reducing substance use may not be as effective as previously thought [4,5,10]. The prevalent approach to adolescent social network interventions for substance use prevention often hinges on the presumption that friendship ties are, to some extent, founded on substance use behaviors. Given that this assumption does not align with our findings, it becomes imperative to investigate culturally relevant alternatives to understanding of how substance use relates to friendship formation. Gaining insight into these alternative predictors is crucial for developing innovative, effective strategies for substance use prevention tailored to AI youth that may center on strengths-based connections rather than social ties rooted in risky behavior.", "page": 16}

trace.raw: {"text": "The absence of consistent substance use effects marks the most striking departure from the broader adolescent network literature. In non-AI samples, substance use homophily and receiver effects are consistently positive and often substantial in magnitude [6,11,13,22] (see Table 1 for a summary of prior findings). By contrast, in our AI-majority sample, substance use showed no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily effects across schools. The only exceptions, alcohol homophily in School B (AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01) and an alcohol sender effect in School C (AME = 0.015, p < 0.05), were isolated and did not replicate across schools or substances. This pattern suggests that substance use operates as a weaker organizing principle for friendship formation in AI reservation schools than in the racially heterogeneous settings that have dominated prior research.", "page": 14}
